title: Knee Pain: Localize the Structure Before Ordering MRI
bottomLine: Knee pain is localized by mechanism, effusion, weight-bearing ability, range of motion and focused ligament/meniscal/patellofemoral examination before imaging. A hot swollen joint, neurovascular injury or major trauma changes the pathway immediately.
recognize: Effusion after trauma raises internal derangement; atraumatic warmth/effusion raises crystal, inflammatory or septic disease.
differentiate: OA, meniscal injury, ligament injury, patellofemoral pain, bursitis and referred hip pain require different management.
assessment: Assess trauma mechanism, locking/giving way, swelling timing, fever, weight bearing, ROM, joint-line tenderness, ligament stability and hip exam when indicated.
workup: Use validated radiograph criteria after acute trauma; MRI is reserved for suspected internal derangement when results will alter management.
Arthrocentesis is urgent when septic arthritis is plausible.
management: Treat stable mechanical disease with activity modification, exercise/physiotherapy and condition-specific analgesia; urgent orthopedic/emergency care for unstable fracture, septic joint or neurovascular compromise.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs require GI/renal/CV risk review; intra-articular steroid should not be given into a joint with possible infection.
redFlags: Hot swollen joint with systemic illness
Unable to bear weight after significant trauma
counselling: Explain why rehabilitation often matters more than immediate MRI in uncomplicated mechanical pain.
followUp: Reassess function and instability; persistent locking or failure of conservative care may warrant imaging/specialty referral.
examTrap: Ordering MRI before localizing the injury or injecting a hot joint before excluding infection.
oneLinePearl: Knee pain becomes easier when you first decide trauma, effusion, instability, or inflammation.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada MSK imaging principles

title: Hip Pain: Joint, Lateral Soft Tissue, Spine, or Fracture?
bottomLine: Hip pain location and function narrow the differential: groin pain suggests intra-articular disease, lateral pain often reflects greater-trochanteric pain, posterior pain may be spinal or deep-gluteal, and inability to bear weight after trauma raises occult fracture concern.
recognize: OA commonly causes activity-related groin pain and reduced internal rotation; fracture may be subtle after low-energy trauma in older adults.
differentiate: Lumbar radiculopathy, bursitis/tendinopathy, avascular necrosis and septic arthritis can mimic hip OA.
assessment: Assess trauma, weight bearing, ROM, gait, groin/lateral/posterior location, fever, steroid/alcohol risk and neurologic symptoms.
workup: Use radiographs for suspected OA/fracture; persistent high fracture suspicion despite negative radiograph requires advanced imaging.
Urgent aspiration/specialty assessment when septic arthritis is possible.
management: Use exercise/physiotherapy, analgesia and risk-factor management for stable degenerative disease; urgent orthopedic care for fracture, septic joint or threatened function.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated corticosteroid exposure without diagnosis and risk review, especially with possible osteonecrosis or infection.
counselling: Teach falls prevention and explain that pain location helps distinguish hip joint disease from spine/soft-tissue causes.
followUp: Reassess mobility and function; refer persistent severe OA or structural disease when surgery may improve function.
examTrap: Calling all lateral hip pain hip-joint OA or dismissing an older adult's fracture because the first radiograph is negative.
oneLinePearl: Groin, lateral hip, and posterior hip pain are different diagnostic neighborhoods.

title: Hand and Wrist Disorders: Tendon, Nerve, Joint, or Fracture?
bottomLine: Hand/wrist complaints are localized by trauma, tendon function, nerve distribution, joint inflammation and vascular status. Snuffbox tenderness, tendon rupture, infection and neurovascular compromise deserve more than a generic wrist-sprain label.
recognize: De Quervain, carpal tunnel, trigger finger, OA/inflammatory arthritis and occult scaphoid fracture have distinct patterns.
differentiate: Median neuropathy differs from cervical radiculopathy and generalized neuropathy; inflammatory polyarthritis differs from isolated overuse pain.
assessment: Assess trauma, swelling, deformity, tendon function, sensory distribution, provocative maneuvers, grip and perfusion.
workup: Use targeted radiographs for trauma; occult scaphoid suspicion requires immobilization and repeat/advanced imaging despite an initial negative study.
Electrodiagnostics are used selectively for uncertain/severe neuropathy.
management: Use splinting/activity modification/therapy for appropriate soft-tissue or nerve syndromes and urgent hand/orthopedic referral for unstable fracture, tendon injury, deep infection or neurovascular compromise.
medicationSafety: Repeated steroid injection carries tendon/skin/nerve risk and should follow diagnosis-specific guidance.
counselling: Teach splint use, ergonomic modification and signs that require urgent reassessment.
followUp: Reassess persistent weakness/numbness, instability or unresolved trauma.
examTrap: Calling a negative initial wrist X-ray reassuring despite classic scaphoid tenderness.
oneLinePearl: A hand exam is anatomy in motion—test the tendon, nerve and bone you suspect.

title: Foot and Ankle Disorders: Weight Bearing, Stability, and Neurovascular Safety
bottomLine: Foot and ankle evaluation starts with mechanism, ability to bear weight, focal bony tenderness, stability and neurovascular status. Use validated radiograph rules for acute injury and do not miss diabetic foot infection, Achilles rupture or compartment/neurovascular emergencies.
recognize: Lateral ankle sprain, Achilles injury, plantar fascia pain, stress injury and fracture have different exam patterns.
differentiate: Cellulitis/gout/Charcot arthropathy can mimic musculoskeletal injury, especially in diabetes/neuropathy.
assessment: Assess mechanism, bony tenderness, swelling, weight bearing, Achilles integrity, pulses/sensation and diabetic ulcer/infection risk.
workup: Use Ottawa ankle/foot principles where applicable; advanced imaging for occult/stress injury or tendon pathology when clinically justified.
management: Functional rehabilitation is preferred for stable sprain; immobilize/refer fractures or tendon rupture as indicated.
Diabetic foot infection or Charcot concern requires prompt multidisciplinary evaluation.
medicationSafety: NSAID choice requires renal/GI/CV risk review; avoid corticosteroid injection into suspected infection.
counselling: Teach protected weight bearing and gradual rehabilitation rather than prolonged unnecessary immobilization.
followUp: Reassess instability, persistent pain or inability to progress weight bearing.
examTrap: Ordering X-rays for every ankle sprain or missing an Achilles rupture because plantar flexion is still possible from other muscles.
oneLinePearl: Foot/ankle triage is weight bearing, focal bone, tendon integrity and circulation.

title: Sports Injuries: Mechanism and Function Before Imaging
bottomLine: Sports injury care is mechanism- and function-driven. Identify fracture/dislocation, concussion, tendon rupture and neurovascular injury first, then use progressive rehabilitation and return-to-sport criteria rather than imaging every painful joint.
recognize: Acute swelling, inability to continue play, instability, focal bony tenderness or neurologic symptoms increase structural-injury concern.
differentiate: Overuse tendinopathy differs from acute tear; muscle strain differs from avulsion/fracture; concussion can occur without loss of consciousness.
assessment: Assess mechanism, immediate symptoms, swelling, ROM, strength, stability, neurologic status and prior injury.
workup: Use validated injury-specific imaging rules; ultrasound/MRI is selected when tendon/ligament diagnosis will change management.
management: Protect serious injury, then use early appropriate loading and physiotherapy for stable injuries; return to sport requires functional recovery, not merely pain improvement.
medicationSafety: Avoid masking serious injury with repeated analgesia while continuing unsafe play; opioid therapy is rarely appropriate for routine sports injury.
counselling: Teach graded return and injury-prevention strategies; concussion return-to-play requires a dedicated protocol.
followUp: Reassess function and sport-specific tasks before clearance.
examTrap: Clearing an athlete because pain is gone despite persistent instability or concussion symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Return to sport is a functional decision, not a pain score.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada MSK imaging principles

title: Tendinopathy and Bursitis: Load the Right Tissue, Do Not Inject the Wrong Diagnosis
bottomLine: Most tendinopathy and noninfectious bursitis are clinical diagnoses treated with activity/load modification and progressive rehabilitation. Acute hot swelling, tendon rupture or systemic illness changes the pathway and corticosteroid injection should never substitute for diagnostic certainty.
recognize: Tendinopathy causes load-related tendon pain and reduced function; bursitis produces focal periarticular tenderness/swelling.
differentiate: Septic bursitis, gout, inflammatory arthritis and tendon tear can mimic routine overuse disease.
assessment: Assess repetitive load, trauma, ROM, resisted strength, swelling/warmth, skin breaks and systemic symptoms.
workup: Imaging is usually unnecessary initially; ultrasound or MRI is reserved for uncertain diagnosis, suspected tear or failure of appropriate rehabilitation.
Aspirate when septic/crystal bursitis is clinically plausible.
management: Use relative activity modification, graded tendon loading/physiotherapy and short-term symptom control.
Treat septic bursitis as infection and refer complete tendon rupture when repair/immobilization decisions are time-sensitive.
medicationSafety: Repeated corticosteroid injection near tendons can weaken tissue; avoid injection into infection or directly into high-risk tendons.
counselling: Explain that tendon recovery requires progressive loading and often takes longer than pain relief.
followUp: Reassess function; persistent symptoms need diagnostic reconsideration rather than serial injections.
examTrap: Injecting a painful swollen bursa before considering infection.
oneLinePearl: Tendon treatment is controlled loading; infection and rupture are different diseases.

title: Ligament Injury: Grade Stability and Protect the Joint
bottomLine: Ligament injury is diagnosed from mechanism, swelling, stability testing and function. The NP must identify unstable injury, associated fracture/dislocation and neurovascular compromise before choosing rehabilitation versus immobilization or surgical referral.
recognize: Rapid swelling and giving-way after pivot injury suggests major knee ligament/internal derangement; ankle inversion injury commonly affects lateral ligaments.
differentiate: Pain-limited guarding can mimic instability; fracture, tendon rupture and meniscal injury can coexist.
assessment: Assess mechanism, immediate swelling, ability to continue activity, joint-line/bony tenderness, stability tests and distal neurovascular function.
workup: Use radiographs according to validated trauma rules and MRI selectively when high-grade ligament/internal derangement diagnosis will change management.
management: Use protection followed by progressive rehabilitation for stable low-grade injuries; refer unstable/high-grade injuries, associated fracture or multi-ligament trauma.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged immobilization without indication because stiffness, weakness and thrombosis risk can increase.
counselling: Teach bracing/rehabilitation and sport-specific return criteria.
followUp: Reassess stability and function after swelling decreases because acute guarding can limit the first exam.
examTrap: Ordering MRI before basic stability/bony assessment or clearing play with unresolved instability.
oneLinePearl: Ligament care is about stability, associated injury and functional recovery.

title: Meniscal Tear: Mechanical Symptoms Matter More Than MRI Words
bottomLine: Meniscal tears are interpreted in clinical context because degenerative MRI findings are common. Locking, recurrent effusion, joint-line symptoms and functional limitation guide management; many degenerative tears improve with exercise-based therapy rather than immediate arthroscopy.
recognize: Twisting injury, joint-line pain, delayed effusion and catching/locking support a meniscal syndrome.
differentiate: OA, ligament injury, patellofemoral pain and loose body can mimic meniscal symptoms.
assessment: Assess trauma, true mechanical locking, effusion, ROM, joint-line tenderness, ligament stability and OA features.
workup: Radiographs assess OA/trauma first when indicated; MRI is reserved for persistent clinically meaningful internal derangement when results will change management.
management: Use physiotherapy/activity modification for most stable/degenerative tears; urgent orthopedic assessment for a truly locked knee or repairable traumatic tear in the appropriate patient.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine opioid therapy and repeated injections as substitutes for rehabilitation/diagnostic reassessment.
counselling: Explain that an MRI tear does not automatically require surgery, particularly with degenerative disease.
followUp: Reassess mechanical symptoms and function after rehabilitation.
examTrap: Sending every degenerative meniscal MRI tear to arthroscopy despite no true mechanical locking.
oneLinePearl: Treat the symptomatic knee, not the incidental MRI tear.

title: Rotator Cuff Disorders: Weakness, Painful Arc, or Tear?
bottomLine: Rotator-cuff disease is localized from active versus passive motion, strength and provocative testing. Acute traumatic weakness, pseudoparalysis or persistent function loss raises tear concern; uncomplicated tendinopathy is initially rehabilitation-based rather than MRI-first.
recognize: Painful arc/night pain and pain with resisted abduction/external rotation support cuff pathology; major weakness after trauma suggests full-thickness tear.
differentiate: Adhesive capsulitis limits active and passive ROM; cervical radiculopathy and referred cardiac disease can mimic shoulder pain.
assessment: Assess trauma, active/passive ROM, strength, neck/neurologic exam and functional demands.
workup: Radiographs are used selectively; ultrasound/MRI when a significant tear is suspected or persistent symptoms would change treatment.
management: Use activity modification, analgesia and progressive physiotherapy for most tendinopathy/partial disease; refer acute major tear, pseudoparalysis or refractory significant dysfunction.
medicationSafety: Corticosteroid injection can provide short-term relief but repeated injections may impair tendon quality and should not replace rehabilitation.
counselling: Teach that strengthening and scapular mechanics are core treatment even when imaging shows degenerative changes.
followUp: Reassess strength/function after rehabilitation and escalate persistent major weakness.
examTrap: Ordering immediate MRI for atraumatic shoulder pain before testing active/passive ROM and strength.
oneLinePearl: Shoulder diagnosis starts with motion and strength before imaging.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada MSK imaging principles
